models.collectorNote: They built 15 million, so rarity is not the value driver, originality and condition are. Brass-era cars (pre-1913) and genuine early production examples are where the money is; a running late T is still one of the cheapest ways into pre-war motoring.

generations.name: Production run
generations.note: Planetary transmission worked by pedals, a hand throttle on the column, and a crank start for most of its life. Ford famously offered it in any color so long as it was black, faster-drying paint kept the line moving.

models.intro: The car that put the world on wheels. Ford built over 15 million of them, cut the price from $850 to under $300, and in doing so invented the moving assembly line's reason to exist. By the early 1920s, roughly half the cars on Earth were Model Ts.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Started as a Falcon underneath with show-car styling on top. The K-code 289 and the big-block GTs made it a genuine performance car; Carroll Shelby's GT350 made it a legend.

generations.name: Second generation (Mustang II)
generations.note: The downsized answer to the fuel crisis: Pinto-based, hatchback offered, and a V8 that returned for 1975 making 122 hp. Collectors mock it; historians note it sold in huge numbers and kept the nameplate alive when the Camaro nearly died.

generations.name: Third generation (Fox body)
generations.note: Light, square, and cheap to make fast. The 5.0 LX with a five-speed is the definitive budget drag car, and the aftermarket that grew around the Fox platform never really went away.

generations.name: Fourth generation (SN-95)
generations.note: A Fox-derived chassis under rounded nineties styling, then the sharper New Edge facelift of 1999. The modular 4.6 replaces the pushrod 5.0; the run peaks with the supercharged SVT Cobra 'Terminator' at 390 hp.

generations.name: Fifth generation (S197)
generations.note: Retro done right: the 1967 fastback redrawn for the modern crash-test era. The Coyote 5.0 arrives in 2011, and the Shelby GT500 closes the run at 662 hp, the most powerful production V8 of its day.

generations.name: Sixth generation (S550)
generations.note: Independent rear suspension at last, right-hand drive, and a genuinely global car. The Shelby GT350's flat-plane-crank Voodoo V8 revs to 8,250 rpm; the Mach 1 and the 760 hp GT500 bookend the range.

generations.name: Seventh generation
generations.note: The last V8 standing in the segment after the Camaro and Challenger died. The GT's Coyote makes 486 hp, and the Dark Horse pushes to 500 with a Tremec six-speed.

models.intro: Launched in April 1964 and sold 22,000 cars on day one. The Mustang invented the pony car, long hood, short deck, endless options list, and has survived gas crises, the Mustang II, and the SUV era without ever leaving production.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Ford's first purpose-built post-war truck, sold as the F-1 through F-8. The flathead V8 and a cab designed around all-day work set the template every truck since has followed.

generations.name: Ninth generation
generations.note: The last of the square, simple F-150s, and the generation that made the SVT Lightning a thing. The 7.3L Power Stroke diesel versions of the heavy-duty trucks are now cult objects.

generations.name: Fourteenth generation
generations.note: Aluminium body, a hybrid PowerBoost option, and the all-electric F-150 Lightning alongside. The twin-turbo V6 outsells the V8, torque won the truck argument years ago.

models.intro: America's best-selling vehicle line for over four decades. The F-Series is less a model than an economy, work truck, family hauler, off-road toy, and status symbol, all on the same ladder frame.

models.collectorNote: GT40 originals trade in the millions and rarely in public. The 2005–2006 GT is the attainable one, still a $400k-plus conversation for low-mile cars, and the 2017 car sits higher again.

generations.name: GT40
generations.note: Forty inches tall at the roof, that's the name. The 7.0-litre Mk II finished 1-2-3 at Le Mans in 1966, and a GT40 won the race four consecutive years. Originals are eight-figure cars.

generations.name: Ford GT, first revival
generations.note: A near-exact silhouette of the GT40 over modern aluminium and a supercharged 5.4. Built 4,038 cars; values roughly tripled and stayed there.

generations.name: Ford GT, second revival
generations.note: Carbon tub, active aero, and a twin-turbo V6 where everyone expected a V8. Won its class at Le Mans in 2016, fifty years after the 1966 win, Ford planned it that way.

models.intro: One nameplate, three separate vendettas against physics. The GT40 was built to beat Ferrari at Le Mans after Enzo walked away from selling to Ford, and did it four years straight, 1966 to 1969. Both modern revivals exist because that grudge never cooled.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Short wheelbase, uncut rear fenders on the good ones, and a V8 option from 1969. Simple enough to fix with hand tools, which is exactly why people pay serious money for them now.

generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: The full-size, F-150-based Bronco, the white one from the 1994 slow-speed chase is a 1993 model. A genuinely comfortable truck that happened to have a removable top.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: Body-on-frame, doors and roof come off, and a Raptor version with long-travel suspension. The 2.7L twin-turbo V6 is the engine to have short of the Raptor.

models.intro: Ford's answer to the Jeep CJ in 1966, a full-size truck-based SUV by the 1980s, dead in 1996, and revived in 2021 as a removable-roof Wrangler rival. The first-generation trucks are the collector sweet spot; the new one is the one you can actually use daily.
